I had been a loyal T-Mobile customer since 2016, when the company introduced its T-Mobile ONE plan. I had a military discount the entire time I was with them, but even with that discount my bill eventually ballooned to $113 a month thanks to T-Mobile’s price hikes. I decided enough was enough, so I started looking for a cheaper alternative. Plus, with Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro costing at least $100 more this year, I thought cutting my cell phone bill might help soften the blow if I upgraded to a new device. And so, I sought out an MVNO.

What is an MVNO?

MVNO stands for “Mobile Virtual Network Operator.” In simple terms, an MVNO is a wireless carrier that doesn’t operate its own nationwide cellular network. Instead, it purchases access to an existing network from one of the major carriers (AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon) and sells that service to its own customers. Think of them as wireless middlemen.

This means that switching to an MVNO doesn’t necessarily mean giving up the network you’re already using. For example, Mint Mobile uses T-Mobile’s network, Visible uses Verizon’s, and US Mobile gives customers the option of using networks from all three major carriers. For the purposes of this article, I’ll be focusing on these three MVNOs because they’re the ones I looked at most closely before leaving T-Mobile, but there are several other options out there as well.

Put simply, an MVNO gives you another way to buy cellular service without necessarily buying it directly from the company that owns the network.

Why are MVNOs cheaper and what’s the “catch?”

If an MVNO can use the same cellular networks as AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, how it can charge so much less? The simple answer is that MVNOs don’t have to shoulder all of the costs associated with operating a nationwide wireless carrier. They don’t have to build and maintain their own networks, many operate primarily online rather than maintaining physical retail locations, and they tend to have fewer employees. These savings can be passed along to customers in the form of lower monthly prices.

MVNOs also tend to offer simpler plans without many of the “perks” and extras that have become common with traditional wireless carriers. Depending on the carrier and plan, you might not get free streaming services or other incentives designed to keep you with a major carrier. But the money you save with an MVNO could easily offset the cost of those “free” perks if you actually want them.

That was certainly the case for me. I always looked forward to the free MLB.TV subscription included with T-Mobile and used it every season, but I never watched Netflix, so the “Netflix on Us” perk was wasted on me. Even if I wanted Netflix and MLB.TV, however, I could simply pay for them myself and still come out ahead with the money I saved by switching. At the end of the day, I mostly just wanted a reliable and more affordable cellular service, and I didn’t need T-Mobile to throw in a bunch of extras to get one.

The “catch” isn’t necessarily that the service is worse. It’s that you’re paying for fewer things. And exactly what you give up depends on the MVNO and plan you choose. Video streaming may be limited to lower resolutions, the amount of high-speed or premium data you get may vary, and network priority can also differ. At home, I have very fast Wi-Fi and rarely find myself in “congested” areas like concerts or stadiums, so network priority was much less of a concern for me in normal, day-to-day use. But I do occasionally travel overseas, so international data was an important factor. Some MVNOs include international data and texting, while others require an additional fee or offer more limited coverage when you travel outside the U.S.

Then there are some less obvious differences, particularly when it comes to buying a new iPhone. Apple Card Monthly Installments and the iPhone Upgrade Program aren’t available when you choose an MVNO as your carrier. If you want to use either of those options, you’re limited to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. In practice, that means you’ll generally need to buy your iPhone outright if you’re purchasing it directly from Apple. The major carriers can also offer large trade-in credits and other promotions that aren’t generally available through MVNOs. Apple Watch support isn’t universal either, so that’s something to check if you have a cellular Apple Watch.

Finally, most MVNOs rely more on phone and chat support than physical stores with face-to-face employees. I consider myself tech-savvy, and I have no desire to wait in line in a store for help. And in my experience, some sales rep in the store is just going to call and get put on hold with the same people I’d end up calling from home anyway so this was not a dealbreaker for me.

The important thing is that none of these are universal limitations of MVNOs. They vary by carrier and plan, which means it’s worth looking at what you’re actually getting before you make the switch.

Three MVNOs worth considering

Once I’d made up my mind to leave T-Mobile, I started looking at alternatives. Postpaid plans on Verizon and AT&T were more expensive than what I was already paying, so both the other two big carriers were a no-go for me. I ultimately narrowed my search down to US Mobile, Mint Mobile, and Visible. Each appealed to me for a different reason, and all three offered a way to significantly lower my monthly wireless bill without giving up access to a major carrier’s network.

US Mobile is perhaps the most flexible of the three, and the carrier I ultimately chose when switching from T-Mobile. That doesn’t mean it’s necessarily the best fit for you, or even the best MVNO of the three. It simply happened to be the best fit for me.

In fact, US Mobile wasn’t my first choice. I hadn’t even heard of the company before I started researching MVNOs. But the more I looked at what it offered, the more it stood out. Here’s why: US Mobile offers service on all three major U.S. networks, allowing customers to choose the network that works best for them. It also offers a Multi-Network add-on that allows you to have two networks active on the same iPhone at the same time, without needing a second phone number. Both networks are tied to your same line, and your iPhone can use whichever network has the better connection for calls and data. So, if T-Mobile’s network works great at the office but Verizon’s works better at home, you can take advantage of both without having to carry two phones or manage two different numbers. US Mobile does charge extra for this feature, and it’s not one I need, but it’s a neat one to have on offer.

I recently moved and was curious how Verizon’s coverage compared with T-Mobile’s near my new home, so I decided to test both networks. I set my wife’s iPhone up on US Mobile’s Light Speed network (which uses T-Mobile) and my iPhone on Warp (which uses Verizon) so we could compare the coverage for ourselves. As it turned out, Verizon was noticeably better in our area, so switching to US Mobile ended up being a win-win: better coverage and significantly less expensive service.

Mint Mobile was my first choice initially because T-Mobile owns it, meaning I could keep using the same network I was already familiar with while paying considerably less for it. What I didn’t like was the lack of included international data. My wife and I like to cruise, and with international travel being a regular part of our lives, having cellular data outside the U.S. is important to us. Mint offers international data, but it comes at an additional cost, which can quickly eat into some of the savings. I also didn’t like that taxes and fees cost extra.

Visible is similarly straightforward, but it runs exclusively on Verizon’s network. My biggest hesitation with Visible was Verizon’s coverage in my area. I had been a T-Mobile customer for nearly a decade, so I knew exactly what to expect from T-Mobile’s network, but I had no idea how Verizon’s coverage would compare. That was really the only thing holding me back from choosing Visible over US Mobile, which gave me the option to try Verizon’s network while still having access to T-Mobile and AT&T if Verizon didn’t work out. Visible also offers a free cellular Apple Watch plan with its highest-tier unlimited plan, which was another appealing feature. (US Mobile offers the same benefit on its highest-tier plan when using Warp, its Verizon network.)

What you’ll need to switch

Switching to an MVNO was easier than I expected. My wife and I kept our existing iPhones and transferred both lines from T-Mobile to US Mobile in about ten minutes. I didn’t even have to leave the couch. You’ll need an unlocked, compatible iPhone (or Android phone, but I am focusing on iPhone) and some information from your current carrier. And if you want to keep your existing phone number, make sure you don’t cancel your old service before the number has been transferred.

Here’s what you’ll need in order to switch:

  • The account number for your current wireless carrier
  • A transfer PIN
  • An unlocked, compatible iPhone
  • A new eSIM
  • A little patience

I paid the upfront annual price for two unlimited plans on US Mobile in preparation for the switch. My wife doesn’t have a cellular Apple Watch and doesn’t care about higher-quality video, so she opted for US Mobile’s Unlimited Starter plan, saving $100 compared with the Unlimited Premium plan that I chose. Paying $500 for two lines with an Apple Watch plan for a year seemed like a great deal compared with the $1,356 per year I was paying T-Mobile for two lines and no Apple Watch service. (And again, just to emphasize, that was with a military discount!)

Generating a transfer PIN through T-Mobile was a straightforward process, which I half-expected to be more buried and complicated than it actually was. Here are the instructions for Verizon and AT&T as well.

With my iPhone connected to Wi-Fi, US Mobile emailed me a new eSIM, and installing it was as simple as tapping a button in the email and following the onscreen instructions. It was the same process for my wife’s iPhone. The only additional step was setting up my Apple Watch, which I was able to do easily through US Mobile’s app.

Why I’m sticking with an MVNO

Same coverage for less money: For the money I’m saving, the concessions I’ve made are more than worth it. I have fast Wi-Fi at home, so cellular data simply isn’t as important to me (though in speed tests, US Mobile’s speeds are just as fast as T-Mobile’s were). What matters most is having a strong, reliable cellular signal when I’m away from Wi-Fi, particularly for making and receiving calls and texts.

No long-term contracts: Most carriers have done away with traditional contract plans, instead shifting to device payment plans that effectively serve the same purpose by keeping you tied to their network until you pay off your phone. I always buy my iPhone directly from Apple because I want the freedom that comes with an unlocked model, but I like that US Mobile, Mint, and Visible don’t require contracts.

Easy to switch: Most MVNOs let you pay month to month, so you aren’t locked into a long-term commitment. If one carrier has a deal one month and another carrier has a better deal the next, it’s quick and easy to switch. There’s also no credit check with prepaid accounts, which means your credit won’t take a hit every time a carrier makes an inquiry, unlike with postpaid accounts, and you can’t be denied because of your credit history. My credit is good, but I still don’t want it to take a hit if I decide to switch from T-Mobile to Verizon and they do a hard inquiry.

Top comment by Zach Chadwick

I was with T-Mobile since 2014. 2 lines was $135 with Device Promotional Trade-in. After Price Hikes and new plans, and trade-in requirements, my bill went up to $185.

I switched to Visible in September 2025. I selected their Pro plan, and I had a promotional code for SAVE26 which gives their best plan for $33/month for 26 months.

Once my mothers trade in credits ended, I switched her over as well. At that time, they had their best plan half off when purchased annually. So a full year of service for $275.

Together this year, I’ll spend $671for both lines. That’s only 4 months of service on T-Mobile.

I haven’t experienced any issues. I have Autopay turned on. They don’t force me to use a debit card or checking account. I’m on 5G UW 90% of the time. I can also stream in 4K with no buffering or lag.

I already created a Visible ‘Circle’ which lets me invite others, and we receive $5/mo per line, which lets me pay everyone’s invoice that’s included within it.

More savings if you pay annually: The trade-off for that flexibility is that you’ll save more if you’re willing to pay for a year of service upfront. Most MVNOs offer a significant discount for annual plans, so you’re giving up some of the freedom to switch whenever you want in exchange for a lower overall price.

No surprise charges: As I mentioned earlier, my wife and I like to cruise. If you’ve ever forgotten to put your iPhone into Airplane Mode on a ship and it connected to the ship’s cellular network, you’re in for a rude awakening and potentially a massive bill. With a prepaid plan, I don’t have to worry about accidentally racking up a massive roaming bill. If international roaming isn’t included, my phone simply won’t connect to an overseas network and charge me for it. Taxes and fees are also included in US Mobile’s plans, so the price listed is the price you’ll actually pay.

Switching to an MVNO wasn’t just about finding the cheapest service I could, but about getting the service I wanted without paying for a bunch of things I didn’t want or need. And so far, I haven’t felt like I’m missing out on anything that matters to me (though I know I will definitely miss the free MLB.TV subscription). In fact, I even gained an Apple Watch line that I didn’t have before while still paying less. I have the same iPhones, the same phone numbers, my coverage is actually better in my area on US Mobile’s Warp (Verizon) network, and I have the freedom to switch again if I find a better option down the road.

Your priorities may be different from mine, and an MVNO won’t necessarily be the right choice for everyone. But if you’re paying a lot for your wireless service and haven’t considered an MVNO, it’s worth taking a look. You might be surprised by how little you actually give up.
